The library lent out sounds in blue tins, each about the size of a peppermint box. Most people borrowed rain. There were fourteen kinds, including rain on a parked car and rain coming through a ceiling into a saucepan. The second was popular with people who had moved away from town and wanted to remember why.

On my first day behind the desk, my aunt showed me how to test a return. You opened the tin just far enough to admit a fingernail. If it was a recording of a horse, you might get a single hoof. If it was a conversation, you might get a word you could spend the rest of the afternoon trying to place.

“Don’t open anything all the way in here,” she said. “A man played a wedding reception once and we had to shout over it until closing.”

I had come home for six weeks to clear out my father’s hardware store. Working at the library gave me somewhere to go when I couldn’t face another drawer full of screws. My father had sorted them by length but not by type, a system I’d complained about when he was alive. Now I kept finding myself holding two screws up to the light, checking whether he’d got it right.

On Thursday, a woman in a green cycling helmet set a tin on the desk.

“Could you put this back without telling Arthur I took it?”

“Who’s Arthur?”

She leaned sideways to see past me. My aunt was in the workroom eating an orange.

“Your father knew me,” she said.

This was how people introduced themselves to me now. Sometimes they’d say it before they said their names.

She was called June. She’d worked at the bakery next door to the hardware store until it closed. The tin she’d returned was labeled *End of the day, Bell Street, 1998*. I knew the year because it was the summer my father put in a new shop door. The old one swelled every August and had to be kicked at the bottom. He’d taken it off its hinges on a Tuesday, and I’d spent the rest of the week kicking the new door out of habit.

“What’s on it?” I asked.

“Mostly me,” June said. “I don’t know why I keep borrowing it. I can hear myself perfectly well at home.”

She tucked her helmet strap under her chin and left. I checked the card in the back of the tin. She’d borrowed it eleven times in three years. Arthur had never borrowed it.

That evening I carried the tin over to the store. I’d sold the counter to a man who planned to turn it into a kitchen island. Without it, the room looked wider and less useful. I sat on the step stool my father wouldn’t let customers use because one of its feet was shorter than the others.

I opened the tin.

A broom scraped the pavement. A bus pulled away. Someone was struggling to collapse a metal display rack, and a woman said, “You’ve got to lift it first.” I recognized June, though her voice was lower then, or perhaps she just had a cigarette in her mouth.

Then came the kick against the door. It made a hollow sound I felt in the toes of my right foot.

“Did you get the milk?” I asked.

I was fifteen. I’d remembered myself at fifteen as nearly grown, but I sounded about nine.

“Ah,” my father said.

“You said you’d get it.”

“I said ah.”

“You always say ah.”

There was a pause. I shifted my weight on the stool. Whatever came next, I thought, might be something I’d forgotten about the two of us. I’d been listening for his voice since he died. Once, in the supermarket, I followed a man who cleared his throat the way my father did, all the way from the freezer aisle to produce.

On the recording my father said, “June, have you got any milk?”

“Not for you.”

“Right,” he said. “I’d better go, then.”

He rattled his keys. I heard him walk away.

June swept for a while. Then she asked me what was wrong.

“Nothing,” I said.

“All right.”

The broom went on scraping. I expected a confession, or at least a sniff. Instead I heard myself ask whether she wanted me to hold the dustpan. She did. The two of us spent some time chasing a piece of cellophane that kept blowing out of it. When we finally caught it, June said, “There you are, you little sod,” with such quiet satisfaction that I laughed aloud in the empty shop.

The tin went silent. I shut it and sat awhile longer. I still didn’t know what had been wrong. It surprised me that there was something about that girl I couldn’t find out just by remembering harder.

The following Thursday, June came in without her helmet. Her hair was flat on one side anyway.

“Who’s Arthur?” I asked her.

“My husband. He thinks I go swimming.”

“Do you?”

“Occasionally. I don’t like to lie outright.”

I got the tin. She turned it over in her hands. The blue paint had worn away at the corners.

“I played it,” I told her.

“Oh, good,” she said. Then she looked at me more closely. “Was that you with the dustpan?”

I said it was.

“Well, I’ve had you down as the paper boy all these years.”

She laughed, and I heard how little her voice had changed. I asked if she wanted to borrow the tin again. She said she’d think about it, and stood at the desk for a bit, looking at the rack of postcards nobody ever bought.

“Did he come back with the milk?” she asked finally.

I didn’t know. But there was a grocery shop still open on the corner, and I hadn’t had tea yet. I asked my aunt to mind the desk and went out to get a pint. When I came back, June had taken off her coat. My aunt had found three cups and was running the hot tap to warm them.

message.reasoning:
**Exploring story ideas**

I need to create a compelling narrative of about 1000 words, with some creative twists, centered around a lost and found theme at a train station. One idea is a "Department of Unfinished Things" that repairs things thought lost. Another could be a town's borrowed library of sounds. 

I want to include a character who's retrieving a recording of her father's shop door—interesting since it also records her as a child. That's a grounded approach. I could also incorporate something about a grandmother's suitcase, or a retiring station caretaker with a lost umbrella. Focusing on the sound library idea seems appealing, with specific family sounds—like a mother’s laugh or a father's whistle—to maintain emotional tension without a tidy resolution. Okay, this could be fun!
